concepts.topicTitle: Acid-Base Indicators and Sensory Properties
concepts.label: Acids, Bases and Indicators
concepts.cardText: Acids are sour in taste and change the colour of blue litmus to red, whereas bases are bitter and change the colour of red litmus to blue. Litmus is a natural indicator, a purple dye extracted from lichen; its colour is purple when it is neither acidic nor basic. Turmeric is another natural indicator, and so are red cabbage leaves and the coloured petals of flowers such as Hydrangea, Petunia and Geranium. A curry stain on a white cloth becomes reddish-brown when soap, which is basic, is scrubbed on it and turns yellow again when washed with plenty of water. Synthetic indicators such as methyl orange and phenolphthalein can also be used. These are called acid-base indicators, or simply indicators.

concepts.topicTitle: Acid-Base Indicators and Sensory Properties
concepts.label: Olfactory Indicators
concepts.cardText: Indicators like litmus tell us whether a substance is acidic or basic by a change in colour. There are some substances whose odour changes in acidic or basic media. These are called olfactory indicators. Finely chopped onion, dilute vanilla essence and clove oil are tested with dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sodium hydroxide: the onion smell is lost in a base but not in an acid, and vanilla and clove oil also change in odour in the same way, so they can be used as olfactory indicators. Acid-base indicators are dyes or mixtures of dyes used to indicate the presence of acids and bases.

concepts.topicTitle: Reactions of Acids and Bases with Metals, Carbonates and Oxides
concepts.label: Reaction of Acids and Bases with Metals
concepts.cardText: When zinc granules are added to dilute sulphuric acid, bubbles of gas form on the surface of the zinc. The gas is hydrogen: it forms bubbles in soap solution, and a burning candle brought near a gas-filled bubble makes it burn. The same happens with hydrochloric acid, nitric acid and acetic acid. The metal displaces hydrogen from the acid as hydrogen gas and forms a compound called a salt, so acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen gas. When a base such as sodium hydroxide is warmed with zinc, hydrogen is formed again, together with sodium zincate. However, such reactions are not possible with all metals. When an acid reacts with a metal, hydrogen gas is evolved and a corresponding salt is formed.

concepts.topicTitle: Reactions of Acids and Bases with Metals, Carbonates and Oxides
concepts.label: Reaction of Metal Carbonates and Hydrogencarbonates with Acids
concepts.cardText: When sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate are each treated with dilute hydrochloric acid, a gas is produced in both cases. Passed through lime water (calcium hydroxide solution), the gas gives a white precipitate of calcium carbonate. On passing excess carbon dioxide, the calcium carbonate reacts further to give calcium hydrogencarbonate, which is soluble in water. Limestone, chalk and marble are different forms of calcium carbonate. All metal carbonates and hydrogencarbonates react with acids to give a corresponding salt, carbon dioxide and water: metal carbonate or hydrogencarbonate + acid gives salt + carbon dioxide + water.

concepts.topicTitle: Reactions of Acids and Bases with Metals, Carbonates and Oxides
concepts.label: Reaction of Metal Oxides with Acids and Non-metal Oxides with Bases
concepts.cardText: When copper oxide is treated with dilute hydrochloric acid, the colour of the solution becomes blue-green and the copper oxide dissolves; the blue-green colour is due to the formation of copper(II) chloride. A metal oxide + acid gives salt + water. Since metallic oxides react with acids to give salts and water, similar to a base reacting with an acid, metallic oxides are said to be basic oxides. Calcium hydroxide, a base, reacts with carbon dioxide to produce a salt and water. Since this is similar to the reaction between a base and an acid, we can conclude that non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature.

concepts.topicTitle: Neutralisation and the Ionic Nature of Acids and Bases
concepts.label: Neutralisation Reaction
concepts.cardText: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added drop by drop to sodium hydroxide solution coloured pink with phenolphthalein, the effect of the base is nullified by the acid and vice-versa, and the pink colour disappears. Acids and bases neutralise each other to form corresponding salts and water.

concepts.topicTitle: Neutralisation and the Ionic Nature of Acids and Bases
concepts.label: What All Acids and All Bases Have in Common
concepts.cardText: All acids generate hydrogen gas on reacting with metals, so hydrogen seems common to all acids. But glucose and alcohol also contain hydrogen and are not acids. In the conductivity activity the bulb glows with hydrochloric and sulphuric acid solutions but not with glucose or alcohol solutions. The glowing of the bulb indicates that there is a flow of electric current through the solution, and the electric current is carried through the acidic solution by ions. Since the cation present in acids is H+, acids produce hydrogen ions, H+(aq), in solution, which are responsible for their acidic properties. Formation of OH-(aq) ions in solution is responsible for the basic nature of a substance.

concepts.topicTitle: Neutralisation and the Ionic Nature of Acids and Bases
concepts.label: What Happens to an Acid or a Base in Water
concepts.cardText: Dry hydrogen chloride gas does not change dry blue litmus paper, but moist blue litmus turns red. This suggests that hydrogen ions in HCl are produced in the presence of water; the separation of H+ ion from HCl molecules cannot occur in the absence of water. Hydrogen ions cannot exist alone, but exist after combining with water molecules, so they must always be shown as H+(aq) or hydronium ion, H3O+. Bases generate hydroxide (OH-) ions in water. Bases which are soluble in water are called alkalis, and all bases do not dissolve in water. Viewing the acid as giving H+(aq) and the base OH-(aq), neutralisation is H+(aq) + OH-(aq) giving H2O(l).

concepts.topicTitle: Concentration, Dilution, and Exothermic Mixing
concepts.label: Dilution and the Heat of Dissolving Acids and Bases
concepts.cardText: The process of dissolving an acid or a base in water is a highly exothermic one: touching the beaker after adding concentrated sulphuric acid or sodium hydroxide pellets to water shows it get warm. Care must be taken while mixing concentrated nitric acid or sulphuric acid with water. The acid must always be added slowly to water with constant stirring. If water is added to a concentrated acid, the heat generated may cause the mixture to splash out and cause burns, and the glass container may break due to excessive local heating. Warning signs are shown on containers of concentrated acids and bases. Mixing an acid or base with water results in a decrease in the concentration of ions (H3O+ or OH-) per unit volume; such a process is called dilution and the acid or the base is said to be diluted.

concepts.topicTitle: The pH Scale and Acid-Base Strength
concepts.label: The pH Scale
concepts.cardText: A universal indicator, a mixture of several indicators, shows different colours at different concentrations of hydrogen ions in a solution. A scale for measuring hydrogen ion concentration, called the pH scale, has been developed. The p in pH stands for potenz in German, meaning power. On the pH scale we can measure pH generally from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very alkaline). The higher the hydronium ion concentration, the lower is the pH value. The pH of a neutral solution is 7, values less than 7 represent an acidic solution, and as the pH value increases from 7 to 14 the OH- ion concentration increases, meaning an increase in the strength of alkali. Paper impregnated with the universal indicator is used for measuring pH.

concepts.topicTitle: The pH Scale and Acid-Base Strength
concepts.label: Strong and Weak Acids and Bases
concepts.cardText: The strength of acids and bases depends on the number of H+ ions and OH- ions produced, respectively. If hydrochloric acid and acetic acid of the same concentration, say one molar, are taken, they produce different amounts of hydrogen ions. Acids that give rise to more H+ ions are said to be strong acids, and acids that give fewer H+ ions are said to be weak acids. In the same way, bases that give more OH- ions are strong bases and those that give fewer are weak bases.

concepts.topicTitle: Importance of pH in Everyday Life
concepts.label: pH in Living Things, Rain and Soil
concepts.cardText: Our body works within the pH range of 7.0 to 7.8, and living organisms can survive only in a narrow range of pH change. When the pH of rain water is less than 5.6, it is called acid rain. When acid rain flows into the rivers, it lowers the pH of the river water, and the survival of aquatic life in such rivers becomes difficult. Plants also require a specific pH range for their healthy growth, which can be checked by testing the pH of the soil with universal indicator paper. The atmosphere of Venus is made of thick clouds of sulphuric acid.

concepts.topicTitle: Importance of pH in Everyday Life
concepts.label: pH in Digestion and Tooth Decay
concepts.cardText: Our stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which helps digest food without harming the stomach. During indigestion the stomach produces too much acid, which causes pain and irritation. To get rid of this pain people use bases called antacids, which neutralise the excess acid; magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia), a mild base, is often used for this purpose. Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth is lower than 5.5. Tooth enamel, made up of calcium hydroxyapatite, is the hardest substance in the body; it does not dissolve in water but is corroded when the pH in the mouth is below 5.5. Bacteria in the mouth produce acids by degradation of sugar and food particles left in the mouth after eating. The best way to prevent this is to clean the mouth after eating. Toothpastes, which are generally basic, neutralise the excess acid and prevent tooth decay.

concepts.topicTitle: Importance of pH in Everyday Life
concepts.label: Self Defence by Animals and Plants Through Chemical Warfare
concepts.cardText: A bee-sting leaves an acid which causes pain and irritation, and a mild base such as baking soda on the stung area gives relief. The stinging hair of nettle leaves injects methanoic acid, causing burning pain. A traditional remedy is rubbing the area with the leaf of the dock plant, which often grows beside the nettle; the dock plant is basic in nature. Natural sources of acids include vinegar (acetic acid), orange and lemon (citric acid), tamarind (tartaric acid), tomato (oxalic acid), sour milk or curd (lactic acid), and ant sting and nettle sting (methanoic acid).

concepts.topicTitle: Salts and Chemicals Derived from Common Salt
concepts.label: Family of Salts and the pH of Salts
concepts.cardText: Salts formed during various reactions can be grouped. Salts having the same positive or negative radicals are said to belong to a family: NaCl and Na2SO4 belong to the family of sodium salts, and NaCl and KCl belong to the family of chloride salts. The pH of a salt depends on the acid and the base it comes from. Salts of a strong acid and a strong base are neutral with pH value of 7. Salts of a strong acid and a weak base are acidic with pH value less than 7, and those of a strong base and a weak acid are basic in nature, with pH value more than 7. Salts have various uses in everyday life and in industries.

concepts.topicTitle: Salts and Chemicals Derived from Common Salt
concepts.label: Common Salt and the Chlor-alkali Process
concepts.cardText: Seawater contains many salts dissolved in it, and sodium chloride is separated from these salts. Deposits of solid salt, often brown due to impurities, are called rock salt; beds of rock salt were formed when seas of bygone ages dried up, and rock salt is mined like coal. Common salt is an important raw material for sodium hydroxide, baking soda, washing soda and bleaching powder. When electricity is passed through an aqueous solution of sodium chloride (brine), it decomposes to form sodium hydroxide. This is called the chlor-alkali process because of the products formed: chlor for chlorine and alkali for sodium hydroxide. Chlorine gas is given off at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode; sodium hydroxide solution is formed near the cathode. All three products are useful.

concepts.topicTitle: Salts and Chemicals Derived from Common Salt
concepts.label: Bleaching Powder
concepts.cardText: Chlorine is produced during the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride (brine), and this chlorine gas is used for the manufacture of bleaching powder. Bleaching powder is produced by the action of chlorine on dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)2. It is represented as Ca(ClO)2, though the actual composition is quite complex. Bleaching powder is used for bleaching cotton and linen in the textile industry, for bleaching wood pulp in paper factories and for bleaching washed clothes in laundry; as an oxidising agent in many chemical industries; and to make drinking water free from germs.

concepts.topicTitle: Salts and Chemicals Derived from Common Salt
concepts.label: Baking Soda
concepts.cardText: Baking soda is commonly used in the kitchen for making tasty crispy pakoras and sometimes for faster cooking. Its chemical name is sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO3), produced using sodium chloride as one of the raw materials. It is a mild non-corrosive basic salt, which is why it can be used to neutralise an acid. On heating it gives sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. Baking powder is a mixture of baking soda and tartaric acid, a weak edible acid; when heated or mixed in water the carbon dioxide produced causes bread or cake to rise, making them soft and spongy. Sodium hydrogencarbonate is also an ingredient in antacids, where being alkaline it neutralises excess acid in the stomach, and it is used in soda-acid fire extinguishers.

concepts.topicTitle: Salts and Chemicals Derived from Common Salt
concepts.label: Washing Soda
concepts.cardText: Washing soda, Na2CO3.10H2O, is another chemical obtained from sodium chloride. Sodium carbonate can be obtained by heating baking soda, and recrystallisation of sodium carbonate gives washing soda. It is also a basic salt. Sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate are useful chemicals for many industrial processes. Washing soda is used in glass, soap and paper industries, in the manufacture of sodium compounds such as borax, and as a cleaning agent for domestic purposes. It is also used for removing permanent hardness of water.

concepts.topicTitle: Water of Crystallisation and Plaster of Paris
concepts.label: Water of Crystallisation
concepts.cardText: Copper sulphate crystals which seem to be dry contain water of crystallisation. When the crystals are heated, this water is removed, water droplets appear in the boiling tube and the salt turns white. If the crystals are moistened again with water, the blue colour reappears. Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt. Five water molecules are present in one formula unit of copper sulphate, whose hydrated formula is CuSO4.5H2O. The Na2CO3.10H2O molecule is therefore not wet; the water is part of the crystal.

concepts.topicTitle: Water of Crystallisation and Plaster of Paris
concepts.label: Plaster of Paris
concepts.cardText: Gypsum, CaSO4.2H2O, is another salt that has water of crystallisation, with two water molecules. On heating gypsum at 373 K it loses water molecules and becomes calcium sulphate hemihydrate, which is called Plaster of Paris, the substance which doctors use as plaster for supporting fractured bones in the right position. Plaster of Paris is a white powder and on mixing with water it changes to gypsum once again, giving a hard solid mass. Only half a water molecule is shown attached because two formula units of CaSO4 share one molecule of water. Plaster of Paris is used for making toys, materials for decoration and for making surfaces smooth.
